TITLE: My Bangla Book — Third Grade (Amar Bangla Boi — Tritiyo Shreni).
PUBLISHER: National Curriculum and Textbook Board, Bangladesh.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: An outdoor scene in front of a red-and-cream school building. Four young children stand and talk among green bushes and white flowers. Three children are closer to the viewer; another stands beside a broad tree on the left. Two butterflies hover near the plants. A leafy decorative border surrounds the page. The title is written in red and green Bengali lettering, with a subtitle in darker lettering. The NCTB emblem appears near the bottom.

TITLE: The National Flag of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
TEXT: The national flag has a solid red circle set against a green rectangular field. The ratio of its length to its width is 10:6. For example, a flag 305 centimeters (10 feet) long is 183 centimeters (6 feet) wide. The red disc's radius is one-fifth of the flag's length. The printed instructions describe positioning the disc by drawing a vertical reference line at nine-twentieths of the length and finding the midline of the width. Common size examples include 305 x 183 cm, 152 x 91 cm and 76 x 46 cm. The final displayed size depends on the building and its requirements.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: At the top is the completed Bangladeshi flag: a saturated green rectangle with a centered-looking red disc displaced slightly toward the hoist. Beneath it, a geometric construction diagram shows a long rectangle divided by horizontal and vertical straight lines. A circle and measurement tick marks are used to illustrate how the position and radius of the red disc are calculated. The diagram is a flag-construction guide, not a mathematical exercise about unrelated circles.

TITLE: National Anthem, followed by the complete text used for singing.
ATTRIBUTION: Rabindranath Tagore.
ENGLISH RENDERING OF MAIN REFRAIN AND VERSES: My golden Bengal, I love you. Forever your sky and your air play a tune in my heart. In spring, the fragrance of mango blossoms fills your groves and makes me feel deeply moved. In the season of ripe crops, the full fields seem to smile sweetly. The shade of the banyan tree and the village riverbanks are soothing. Your words, Mother, sound like nectar to me. When sadness clouds your face, tears fill my eyes. The page prints the short national-anthem passage and a longer version for singing, repeating images of Bengal as a beloved mother, fields, seasons and landscape.
NOTE: This is a meaning-based English rendering, not a line-for-line singable translation of the full Bengali lyric.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A decorative pale blue and pale green border with small bird and leaf designs; all central content is anthem text with a horizontal rule dividing the short passage from the longer singing text.

TITLE: My Bangla Book — Third Grade.
TEXT: This is the Bengali textbook designated by the National Curriculum and Textbook Board for Grade 3 under the 2014 curriculum. The National Curriculum and Textbook Board, Bangladesh, is the publisher.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Mostly white title page with the title in prominent green and red Bengali letters, the grade in blue, a faded plant emblem in the center and the NCTB seal at lower left.

TEXT: National Curriculum and Textbook Board, Bangladesh, at 69–70 Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka 1000. The book lists its writers and editors, educational guidance, picture designers and illustrators, and publication history. TITLE: Preface.
TEXT: Primary education is the foundation of later learning. If primary education is not well planned and goal-directed, the entire education system is weakened. Bangladesh's 2010 education policy therefore gave special importance to the primary level. It stressed improving and widening access to primary education, including children across social class, economic circumstance, religion, ethnicity and gender. NCTB designed an integrated curriculum to bring together educational research, international experience and Bangladesh's own values of learning and teaching. The aim is practical, life-centered, effective and enjoyable education. Textbooks are essential tools for implementing the curriculum. Authors and editors therefore consider curricular objectives, children's curiosity and their capacity to learn. The books should nurture patriotism and moral values along with literacy. The Grade 3 text builds on work in Grade 1 and Grade 2, repeats selected familiar words and characters for continuity, and gradually strengthens language knowledge. The preface thanks those responsible for writing and illustrating the book; notes revisions following the changed situation of 2024; acknowledges possible errors; and welcomes thoughtful suggestions.
SIGNED: Professor Rabiul Kabir Chowdhury, Acting Chairman, NCTB, September 2025 (name as read from the page).
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: The heading and signature block are green or bolded; this is a text-heavy preface page with ornamental branches and small birds at the margins.

LESSON: Our Conversation.
STORY: Today is the first day of school. Everyone has advanced to a new class and feels happy. The narrator is Raju. He studies in Class 3. His friends include Tithi, Mitu, Jhimith and many others. Raju is holding a new Bangla book. Reading a new book is fun, and the friends look forward to reading and enjoying themselves together.
DIALOGUE: Tithi asks Jhimith, "How are you?" Jhimith says, "I am fine. How are you?" Tithi says that she is fine too, then asks where Mitu is, because she cannot see her.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four uniformed children gather by the schoolyard flower bed. A smiling boy in a white shirt stands to the left, a taller girl in a blue uniform stands beside him, another schoolgirl with a teal shoulder bag stands near the center, and a boy in a white shirt raises an arm to greet his friends on the right. The brick school entrance and a row of flowers appear behind and in front of them.

DIALOGUE CONTINUED: Jhimith points out Mitu and calls her over. Mitu asks how everyone is doing. Tithi says they are well and that she has brought something for her friends. They ask what it is. Tithi says she brought chocolates. Mitu is delighted. Jhimith suggests sharing and eating them together. Mitu thanks Tithi, and Tithi thanks all her friends.
EXERCISE: Fill in the blanks with the correct words from the word bank: fine/good, you, friend, thanks and third.
(a) I study in the ___ grade. (b) I have many ___. (c) My name is ___. (d) How are ___? (e) I offer you my ___. [A few blank sentences are reconstructed from the visibly printed word bank and preceding text; the OCR is incomplete.]

LESSON: Our Family and Our Neighbours.
TEXT: "I am Raju. There are two children in our family, a brother and a sister. I study in Grade 3. My sister Tuli studies in Grade 5. We go to school together." "My father is a farmer. He grows different crops in the fields." "We have a duck and chicken farm. My mother takes care of it."
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTIONS: Four separately captioned square pictures arranged in a two-by-two grid. Upper left: Raju and Tuli walk on green grass before a multistory school building, carrying their school bags. Upper right: a girl and boy walk together toward another large school building bearing a nameboard and Bangladesh flag. Lower left: a farmer in a checked shirt walks through a green crop field with a basket or farming equipment, with agricultural plants on either side. Lower right: a woman sits beside ducks and chickens around their outdoor farm enclosure, with houses and trees behind her. Each picture directly corresponds to the short text below it.

TEXT: "Mitu is our neighbour. Mitu has two sisters in her family. Her elder sister goes to high school. She loves us and often tells us interesting stories." "Mitu's father runs a bookshop called Pubali Library. Many enjoyable books are available there." "Mitu's mother works as a nurse in a hospital. She helps care for sick people in our village." "Around us live people who do many different kinds of work. We all live together in harmony."
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTIONS: Upper left: two girls walk together along a village path near huts, trees and grass, illustrating the neighbour and older sister. Upper right: a busy roadside bookshop or market stall, illustrating the bookstore. Lower left: a nurse wearing a white uniform assists a young schoolgirl outside a hospital building, illustrating nursing as a profession. Lower right: a diverse group of adults and children in work clothes stands together, representing different occupations and living peacefully with neighbours.

EXERCISE 1: Find these words in the lesson: fifth, crop, farm, neighbour, nurse, profession.
EXERCISE 2: Complete the sentences with the vocabulary words. (a) After two more years, I will advance to the ___ grade. (b) Her home has a ___ [as indicated by the source word bank]. (c) Farmers grow ___ in the field. (d) My father's ___ is farming. (e) We all live in ___.
EXERCISE 3: Speak and write answers. (a) What does Raju's father do? (b) Who looks after the duck and chicken farm? (c) Where does Mitu's mother work? (d) Name three professions.
EXERCISE 4: Say what you want to become when you grow up.

LESSON: The Rubbish Box. Format: a four-panel illustrated conversation.
PANEL 1: An elderly man tells shopkeeper Harun, "Please understand, she is my granddaughter. She has come to visit." Harun stands behind the counter of a small roadside shop, and the grandfather sits on a stool with a little girl in pink beside him.
PANEL 2: Harun asks the girl, "What is your name?" She replies, "My name is Reba." He then asks whether Reba wants something from his shop. She answers politely, "No, uncle, thank you."
PANEL 3: A boy asks Harun to give him a banana. A bunch of bananas hangs from the stall roof.
PANEL 4: The boy in a blue shirt eats the peeled banana, with repeated eating sounds, "Gop, gop, gop."
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four frames form a two-by-two comic page. Most scenes are set in front of a corrugated-roof roadside shop with jars on a red cloth, a wooden counter, and bananas hanging near the doorway. The grandfather is elderly with white hair, glasses and a pale-yellow long tunic; Reba has dark pigtails and a pink-purple dress.

section: The Rubbish Box. Format: a four-panel illustrated conversation.
text:
PANEL 1: Reba notices a discarded banana skin beside the shop. Her thought is: "Someone could slip on a banana peel."
PANEL 2: Another boy says to Harun, "Uncle Harun, please give me a packet of biscuits." Harun passes a blue packet from his shop counter.
PANEL 3: The boy in a green shirt eats the biscuits. His chewing is shown as "crunch, crunch, crunch."
PANEL 4: The boy throws away his wrapper near the already discarded banana skin. Reba thinks or says, "Everyone seems to be throwing rubbish everywhere."
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Top left shows the banana skin directly in front of the counter, near Reba's feet. Top right shows a boy buying a packet of biscuits. Bottom left is a close-up of the boy eating while holding the blue wrapper. Bottom right shows both the discarded wrapper and the banana peel lying on the bare ground while Reba looks disappointed.

section: The Rubbish Box. Format: a four-panel illustrated conversation.
text:
PANEL 1: Reba politely asks Harun for two boxes. He asks, "What sort of boxes?"
PANEL 2: Reba replies, "Two large cardboard boxes and a pen will do." Harun hands a cardboard box to her.
PANEL 3: Reba sits on a low stool and writes a label on the boxes. The words on the front identify rubbish containers.
PANEL 4: She places two labelled boxes on the ground beside Harun's shop, where the litter was earlier thrown.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four sequential comic frames. Reba requests materials, accepts a brown cardboard box, writes on it with a pen, and places two brown boxes beside the counter. One box is intended for banana peels and similar food waste, and the other for other rubbish. The cardboard boxes are ordinary improvised bins rather than large manufactured wastebaskets.

section: The Rubbish Box. Format: a four-panel illustrated conversation.
text:
PANEL 1: Reba explains, "Banana peels must be thrown into this box, and other rubbish into the other box." The two boxes are clearly visible on the floor.
PANEL 2: Another child politely asks the shopkeeper for a banana.
PANEL 3: The grandfather points to the boxes and says that peels should go into that rubbish box. Reba watches as a child uses the box rather than littering the ground.
PANEL 4: Reba points out the bins to a new visitor and says: "Bin! The box for putting rubbish!"
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four panels show the bins being explained and used by different customers. Two cardboard boxes sit side by side, one containing banana peel and the other blue food packaging. The stall's jars and bananas provide visual continuity with earlier pages.

section: The Rubbish Box. Format: a four-panel illustrated conversation.
text:
PANEL 1: Reba has an idea while looking at the shop, grandfather and rubbish boxes. A thought bubble says, "I have thought of something."
PANEL 2: A short time later, she returns with a brown goat on a rope and stands beside the two boxes.
PANEL 3: The goat bends its head into the box of banana peels and eats the peels. Reba encourages it with "Eat."
PANEL 4: Harun says, "Wonderful work! The front of my shop will not get dirty anymore."
LESSON MESSAGE: Keep shared places clean, do not throw food waste or wrappers on the ground, and provide proper places for rubbish. The goat is an illustration in this particular story, not a general instruction that all rubbish should be fed to animals.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four comic frames. Reba changes into an orange dress and white trousers, and the goat eats banana peels. In the final panel, Harun gestures approvingly; the grandfather and girl in pink sit to one side; the cardboard boxes are visible by the counter.

LESSON: The Grasshopper and the Ant.
STORY: It is a sunny autumn afternoon. A grasshopper hops and plays in the grass. It notices an ant pulling a large burden under the hot sun. The grasshopper tells the ant that the day is beautiful, and asks why it is working instead of coming to play. The ant continues its work.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Large colorful scene of an oversized green grasshopper on a reddish mound and a small brown ant at the left, carrying a bulky load. The insects have expressive eyes. Bright green grass, small flowers and a soft blue cloud-shaped background create a storybook setting. The size difference emphasizes the two characters.

STORY CONTINUED: The ant explains that winter will come soon, and it is collecting food while the weather is warm because it will not be able to leave home easily later. The grasshopper laughs and says winter is still far away. It invites the ant to play. The ant replies that each must do their own work. Thinking the ant foolish, the grasshopper keeps hopping, playing and singing. Winter finally arrives: sunlight weakens and fog spreads. The grasshopper can find neither food nor a way to play comfortably. Hungry, it visits the ant and asks for something to eat. The ant says it has saved its own food, not the grasshopper's, and asks why the grasshopper did not save food in the warm season. The grasshopper says it spent the time playing and singing. The ant replies that if important work is not done at the proper time, suffering follows.
VOCABULARY: Autumn = a season including the Bengali months Bhadra and Ashwin. Winter = a season including Poush and Magh. "Save/collect" = store for later use.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: The ant stands next to an open wooden food chest full of gathered brown round food items. A green grasshopper looks on from a mound at right. Nearby grass and small seed-like objects show the food that was gathered.

EXERCISE 1: Separate the joined Bengali consonants in words meaning "ask," "hunger," "savings" and "hardship" (jiggasha, khudha, sonchoy, koshto), and use each conjunct in another word.
EXERCISE 2: Put the jumbled events in order: winter arrived; the warmth of the sun decreased; fog covered the surroundings; the grasshopper found no food; it could no longer play.
EXERCISE 3: Answer orally and in writing. (a) What was the ant doing in the sunshine? (b) What was the grasshopper doing? (c) Why did the grasshopper visit the ant's home? (d) Which of them was foolish, the ant or the grasshopper?
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Letter-splitting examples, five lines for ordering events, and four short-answer comprehension prompts. There is no separate animal scene.

section: I Will Become. AUTHOR: Kazi Nazrul Islam.

LESSON: The Frog's Punishment.
STORY: One day the forest is thrown into disorder. An ant marches into the king's court and complains that a hen has destroyed its home. The king summons the hen. The hen says that a snake broke its egg, so it rushed to catch the snake and unintentionally disturbed the ant's nest. The king's soldiers bring in the snake. The snake says its tail has been hurt because a deer stepped on it. The frightened deer is summoned and blames a crane: the crane suddenly flapped its wings, causing the deer to jump and step on the snake.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: At upper left a crowned lion-like forest king sits on a wooden throne. A red ant stands before him. Down the right margin are small paintings of a running hen, a green snake, and a man holding a stick alongside a deer. Their placement follows the chain of animals summoned to court.

STORY CONTINUED: The soldiers bring in the crane. It says that a bulbul startled it, making it cough and flap its wings. The bulbul says it had heard there would be a storm and was worried. The rumour of the storm came from the frog, who had frightened others with an untrue warning. It had not stormed. Soldiers eventually find the frog hiding in a hole beneath a tree. Its legs stick out from the hole, so they pull it out and carry it to court. The king asks why the frog spread the false report. The frog says it had visited town, had heard talk about a storm, and passed the story on to the bulbul. The king punishes the frog, and the story explains the spots on a frog's body as marks of this punishment. The central lesson is not to spread rumours without checking whether they are true.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four small pictures along the right: a colorful long-beaked bird in flight (the crane), a dark tree-root hollow where the frog hides, a branch carrying leaves and nests or fruit, and a green spotted frog sitting among leaves near the ground. The text wraps around the scenes.

VOCABULARY: soldier = a member of the king's guard; rumour = false or unverified information; to spread a rumour = to pass it around; whip = a stick with a cord or strap used for striking.
EXERCISE 1: Find these words in the story and explain them: court, soldier, rumour, whip, spread.
EXERCISE 2: Fill in blanks: "Two ___ are guarding"; "A ___ is needed to drive a horse"; "Although the news was true, someone spread it as a ___." (The original Bengali grammar determines the final forms.)
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A vocabulary list and two writing exercises; no new illustrated scene.

EXERCISE 3: Choose and write the correct answer. Which punctuation mark ends a question? Where did the ant go? [Choices: near town, an earthen hole, under a jackfruit tree, the king's court.] Whose tail was bleeding? [Choices include deer and snake.] Where had the frog travelled? [Choices include the hen's home, a hole, village and city.]
EXERCISE 4: Speak and write. (a) Why did the ant go to the royal court? (b) Who broke the hen's egg? (c) Where did the bulbul enter or hide? (d) How did spots appear on the frog's body in the story?

LESSON: Read and Write Sentences.
READ: A child says to an aunt, "Auntie, thank you very much." The aunt or mother answers that she will come again. Another brief exchange says, "What a beautiful morning!" and "Ah, how painful when someone gets hurt!" The page uses address words such as mother, auntie, friend and uncle and models natural exclamation and conversation.
WRITE: Copy or extend the partially completed replies to the speech examples. In another illustrated scene, a child admires the morning scenery and one responds to heavy rainfall: "What heavy rain!"
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTIONS: Right upper illustration shows an adult man in a green kurta speaking kindly to a young girl in pink. Middle illustration is a sunrise over a village pond, trees, grass and grazing cattle. Lower illustration shows dark rainclouds and rainfall over a green rural hut beside water. Sentences and blank rules align with the pictures.

LESSON: A Joyful Day.
STORY: When the class bell rings, the teacher arrives with good news: the class will go on a school excursion. The children cheer. The teacher asks where they should go, listens to their opinions and learns that most students want to visit Lalbagh Fort. They decide to go on the following Saturday. Mili says she cannot go because walking is difficult for her. Tuli reassures Mili: "So what? We are here and will help you." The teacher allocates responsibilities. She tells everyone to arrive before 10 in the morning, wear school uniforms and bring water, a pen and a notebook.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A teacher wearing a pink sari stands at the right with a green book in one arm and greets a group of children. A smiling boy waves, a schoolgirl with a braid raises her hand, and students sit at desks in the background. The illustration emphasizes inclusion and friendly classroom discussion.

STORY CONTINUED: The children queue and board a vehicle one by one. The teacher asks Raju to record everyone's names. Tuli and other students help Mili get on. Everyone enjoys the journey. When the vehicle reaches Lalbagh Fort, the teacher tells the class to get down slowly. She shows them around and the children take notes. They observe the main gateway, flower garden, three-domed mosque, pond, museum, mound, coins, and old coins from earlier periods.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION 1: A detailed colored view of Lalbagh Fort, a long reddish Mughal-era brick structure with an imposing central arch, domes, towers, smaller side arches and lawns in front.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION 2: A wooden signboard stands among flowers, identifying an area or visitor instruction near the fort. Beneath and beside the fort picture is a vertically arranged list of features seen during the visit.

STORY CONTINUED: After viewing the fort, the teacher gathers everyone in a circle on the grounds and asks how they enjoyed the visit. They answer, "Very much." She asks who will sing; Mitu and Raju sing songs. When it is time to return, everyone queues to board the vehicle. Raju checks names against his list, the bus starts and they return. The class has had a joyful day.
VOCABULARY: museum = a place that preserves and displays historically important objects; children's park = place for children's recreation; fort = defensive structure built against enemy attack; responsibility = assigned work; notebook = small writing book; gate = main entrance; dome = rounded roof; mound = raised land; ancient = old; coin = piece of money made of metal.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: No large drawing; the lower half of the page is a two-column glossary.

EXERCISE 1: Write sentences with opinion, museum, notebook, ancient and list.
EXERCISE 2: Break Bengali joined consonant letters into component letters and form other words using examples from "fort," "bell," "dome," "joy," "class," "responsibility," and "coin."
EXERCISE 3: Answer. (a) Why did the children cheer in class? (b) Where did they agree to go together? (c) What did the teacher tell them to bring? (d) Who was asked to keep a list of names?
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Spelling practice and comprehension worksheet with several empty ruled lines.

EXERCISE 4: Read different sentence types. "Please give me some water" is a request. "Everyone take out your notebooks" is an instruction. "You should help other people" is advice. "Have you finished your homework?" is a question.
EXERCISE 5: Plan a class excursion together. Answer where you will go, when, with whom, how you will travel, what you will do, when you will leave and when you will return.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A short comparison of sentence functions followed by a simple itinerary template: seven prompts with dotted lines.

LESSON: A Day on the Sandbar.
STORY: Far from Dhaka lies a small village named Achinpur. Tithi's family lives there and she visits during the summer holiday. She enjoys seeing greenery, trees, birds flying in the sky and the morning sun peeking through rows of betel nut palms. A river runs beside the village. Nader Uncle, a fisherman, has told her about the many birds that gather on a sandy river island. Boatman Ganesh Uncle says white egrets wait quietly and suddenly catch fish. Tithi longs to see these birds herself. One morning Ganesh arrives with a boat and her father agrees to go. They pass the potters' neighborhood. Her father's friend Madhu Pal, who makes decorative clay pots, joins them and shows Tithi beautiful colorful pots.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Tithi, in an orange-and-pink dress with dark braids, stands under a broad tree and extends her arms toward the river. The broad scene includes green paddy fields, a sandy opposite bank, a moored wooden boat and small thatched-roof houses, establishing the village riverside setting.

STORY CONTINUED: As the boat goes farther, village schoolteacher Hamid Uncle calls from the shore. Ganesh stops and Tithi's father invites him aboard. The boat starts again. Tithi carefully touches the clear, cool river water. They soon reach a sandbar like a beautiful little island. Thorny bushes, grass and tall white reed plants cover it. Mynas pick at insects. A white egret stands on one leg, with its neck bent. A kingfisher sits in the tall reeds. A flock of gulls flies in from the east and Tithi marvels at the sight. Nader Uncle approaches from the western side carrying freshly caught fish, some still moving. He invites everyone to lunch. Ganesh says they must return. Hamid sees clouds gathering in the northeastern sky and a cool wind rising over the river. Everyone boards quickly. Ganesh and Nader row hard. Just as they near the shore a storm begins. Tithi wonders how the birds are coping.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A long narrow boat carries passengers through blue river water near a wide grassy sandbar. White birds fly overhead; a mass of tall reeds rises at the right edge, and low green land extends into the distance.

VOCABULARY: to peek = to look from behind something; rain = badal; sandbar or char = sandy land created in a river; reed (nolkhaagra) = tall, tube-like grass; minar = tower.
EXERCISE 1: Find and explain peek, tower, rain, sandbar and reeds.
EXERCISE 2: Complete sentences using words meaning stream, bird, sandbar and similar vocabulary: "The river water is ___"; "The birds come from ___"; "As the water level decreased, a ___ emerged in the river"; "A ___ is sitting on a tree branch."
EXERCISE 3: Match halves of the sentences: morning sun peeks through betel-nut trees; many birds gather on the river sandbar; water sparkles; the white egret stands on one leg with its neck bent.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Vocabulary and fill-in worksheets. A four-cell word bank and several long underlines, no new scene drawing.

EXERCISE 4: Learn opposites; examples include far/near, white/black, quiet/noisy, land/water and other printed paired antonyms.
EXERCISE 5: Choose the correct answers. What is Tithi's village called? [Options: Madhupur, Achinpur, Shafipur, Nazirpur.] Who is the boatman? [Choices: Nader, Hamid, Madhu, Ganesh.] Who makes pottery? [Choices drawn from the four uncles.] Which bird sits quietly in the reeds? [Options: kingfisher, gull, myna, egret.] Identify the earlier or later event in the provided sentence set.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A pair of small two-column antonym tables and four-choice reading comprehension questions.

EXPLANATIONS: Potters' quarter (kumarpara) = a locality where potters live together; island = a body of land surrounded by water on all sides.
EXERCISE 7: Answer aloud and write. (a) How does Tithi feel about the village's natural surroundings? (b) Where did the group go by boat? (c) Which fish were in Nader Uncle's basket? (d) Why did Tithi worry about the birds? (e) What do birds do during a storm?
EXERCISE 8: Insert proper punctuation: "Tithi has come to visit the village"; "What a cold wind"; "Where does Tithi live"; "Ganesh Uncle said we must return."
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A sequence of question and punctuation exercises with alphabetic question markers; no new full-size scene.

section: Our Village. POET: Bande Ali Miah.
text:
LESSON: Our Village. POET: Bande Ali Miah.
POEM — ENGLISH RENDERING OF MAIN IDEAS: Our little village has small houses. Everyone in the neighborhood lives together like relatives; people read, play and share experiences. Children go to school and respect their elders. The villagers avoid quarrels and jealousy. The village pond is filled with water; sunlight makes it sparkle. Mango trees, jamun trees and bamboo groves stand together as if members of one family. The golden sun rises in the east. Birds call, the breeze moves and flowers bloom. [Some verse lines on the illustrated page are not reliably legible; this passage represents the readable poem's meaning.]

A wide river and small wooden boats run behind them.

LESSON: A Land of Rivers.
TEXT: Bangladesh is a country of rivers. Hundreds of rivers spread across it like a network. Some have wonderful names. Agunmukha sounds like "fire-mouth" though it does not contain fire. Dudh Kumar means "milk boy." Smaller rivers include Dhantara and Dhanshiri, names associated with paddy. Among larger rivers are the Padma, Meghna, Jamuna and Brahmaputra. Some rivers wind, others run straight; some are calm and some have fast currents. The book traces the Brahmaputra to the Himalayas and likewise associates the Padma with the Himalayas. The Padma is famous for hilsa fish. The Jamuna is known for big baghair fish. Dolphins were once frequently seen in the Meghna, which joins the Bay of Bengal. The Atrai is unusual for going from Bangladesh into India and returning. The Naf separates Bangladesh and Myanmar.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A sweeping landscape across the top: broad blue river water, a grassy bank, and several wooden boats with curved woven canopies. Reeds stand prominently in the left foreground. The river runs toward a distant green tree-lined horizon.

STORY CONTINUED: The Karnaphuli River enters Bangladesh after originating in India's Lushai Hills and has a strong current. The Halda River is loved by breeding fish because mother fish go there to lay eggs. Some rivers flow through forests; examples include Harintana, Baleshwar and Nilkamal. Some are home to unusual animals and fish. Someshwari winds like a snake and brings sand. During mountain floods, the Piyain carries both small and large stones. Even small rivers can be powerful. Sadly, these beautiful rivers are becoming polluted. People throw polythene, waste and rubbish into them. Some rivers have become so dirty that clean usable water is scarce. People also fill rivers with land and place barriers upstream, causing waterways to die. Rivers must be protected because protecting the rivers also protects Bangladesh.
VOCABULARY: current = movement of river water; fast-flowing = having strong current; polluted = damaged by contamination; dolphin = a marine/aquatic mammal; famous = widely known; harmless = peaceful or not harmful.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A river with orange-brown shallows and wide blue stretches winds toward a low horizon. A slim wooden boat is stranded or resting on exposed sand or shallow water. Vegetation and the opposite bank appear in the distance. The lower landscape highlights a river's changing depth and width.

EXERCISE 1: Make sentences with river current, calm, desire or hobby, strength and peace.
EXERCISE 2: Choose the correct answer. Which is a small river? [Padma, Meghna, Dhantara, Jamuna.] Which river originates in the Himalayas according to the passage? [Padma, Karnaphuli, Jamuna, Atrai.] Which river separates Bangladesh and Myanmar? [Karnaphuli, Naf, Piyain, Buriganga.] Which river was described as visiting a neighbouring country and returning? [Atrai, Jamuna, Halda, Dhaleshwari.] Identify the string of letters that cannot be rearranged into a valid word.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four-choice selection questions and a set of empty sentence lines, arranged in a text-only worksheet.

EXERCISE 3: Match sentence beginnings with river names: Padma begins in the Himalayas (as stated by the book); Meghna meets the Bay of Bengal; Karnaphuli comes from the Lushai Hills; Halda is a spawning place for mother fish; Someshwari bends like a snake; Piyain carries stones. section: A Story of Winning and Losing.
text:
LESSON: A Story of Winning and Losing.
STORY: A boy stands in the classroom doorway, leaning on crutches. Teacher Noman invites him in. His name is Rashed, and he has newly enrolled. The teacher remembers that Rashed answered questions quickly on admission day and appeared very bright. Noman introduces him to the class and explains that Rashed will study with the other children. The class is discussing an upcoming sports competition. Children can choose different events, and Rashed wants to take part too. The story centers on determination, inclusion, equal respect and taking part rather than assuming that a child who uses crutches cannot compete.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Teacher Noman is depicted in a long-sleeved green shirt with one arm extended, speaking to a boy in a white school shirt at the front of a classroom. Other children in white and blue uniforms sit at brown desks in the background.

section: A Story of Winning and Losing.
text:
STORY CONTINUED: Three days later the sports ground is decorated with colored paper and everyone is excited. The first event is a mathematics race: solve a sum and then run. Rashed is quick at mathematics. The problem is 95 minus 67. He writes 28, takes his crutches and moves quickly toward the finish line. Competitors are ahead and behind him, but Rashed reaches the finish and wins. Next is a game called "cockfight," in which players balance and jostle one another, typically while holding their arms behind them. Rashed puts his crutches aside and prepares. Eight players begin. He avoids attacking impulsively and instead protects himself. Five players fall. The remaining players are Rashed, Raju and Jhimith. Raju approaches Rashed; Rashed moves away and Raju loses his balance.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Four schoolboys wearing white short-sleeved shirts and blue shorts are shown on a grassy field. In the central pair, one boy braces his arms and shoulders while facing another. A boy at the right appears mid-hop. The picture illustrates the balancing-and-bumping game rather than an actual fight between chickens.

section: A Story of Winning and Losing.
text:
STORY CONTINUED: The game is now between Rashed and Jhimith. Jhimith charges. Rashed moves aside and blocks with his shoulder. At one point he nearly falls but regains his balance with determination. Jhimith attacks again. Rashed makes a small shoulder movement and steps away; Jhimith tumbles to the ground. The children shout Rashed's name. The story illustrates that skill, strategy and confidence can matter more than assumptions about physical ability.
VOCABULARY: sports = games and physical competitions; quickly = promptly; anxiety = worry about what may happen; rapidly = at high speed; firm/determined = strong; attack = move against an opponent in an attempt to win.
EXERCISE 1: Find and explain words meaning sport, quick, anxiety, fast and determined.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: This page is mostly story text and short word definitions, without an independent large colored illustration.

LESSON: Laughter. POET: Roknuzzaman Khan.
POEM — ENGLISH RENDERING: Does anyone really know how to laugh? Brother, let me tell you some amusing news. Little Khokon laughs with his toothless mouth; the moon seems to laugh with him. Water lilies bloom laughing in the dark lake, and the duck laughs too. Seeing the laughter of the khalsha fish, the parrot begins to laugh. The parrot laughs with its red beak. The heron, the cuckoo and the myna laugh, and the owl laughs at them as well. The boal fish has such a startling laugh that one's heart leaps in surprise. Yet those who look permanently stern finally cannot resist smiling either. [Meaning-based prose version of the verse, rather than matching its sound and rhymes.]

A large open-mouthed blue-gray catfish rises from water in the lower-left foreground. On the right, a happy child appears above a colorful river scene: a small fish leaps from water, a duck laughs with its beak open, and a bright green parrot with a red beak perches on a branch. Text runs down the middle between these images.

LESSON: Our Festivals.
TEXT: A festival is a joyful celebration. Different communities have their own festivals. Some express love for the country; others are family occasions; others have religious or regional significance. The first day of the Bangla year is Pohela Boishakh. People welcome the new year, celebrate with fairs in towns and villages, buy toys and traditional things such as clay and wooden horses and dolls, and take part in processions. Hill communities also celebrate the new year, including a festival collectively called Boisabi. People gather flowers, cook special mixed vegetable dishes and arrange games. Muslims celebrate Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha. Families attend Eid prayers, prepare foods such as firni, semai and polao, visit one another and embrace.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION 1: Three smiling young people wearing bright blue, red and purple hold decorative painted masks and a colorful paper windmill while celebrating Bangla New Year.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION 2: Two Muslim men in traditional caps greet with an embrace outside a red-domed mosque under a crescent moon.

TEXT CONTINUED: Hindus celebrate Durga Puja, one of their largest religious festivals, in the autumn. People wear festive clothes and visit decorated worship pavilions, where music, drums and prayers accompany the occasion. Christians observe Christmas on December 25, decorate Christmas trees, sing and celebrate the birth of Jesus. Buddhists celebrate Buddha Purnima with visits to monasteries, flowers, colored paper decorations, prayers and lamps. There are also family and social celebrations, including birthdays and weddings. The different celebrations make people happy and help communities live together with understanding and friendship.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION 1: A woman in a white sari with red borders and a child carry offerings or festive items toward a colorful Durga image in the background.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION 2: Two children wearing red Santa hats decorate a green Christmas tree with ornaments and a star.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION 3: Two Buddhist worshippers kneel or bow before a seated golden Buddha statue on a raised platform. Each illustration is next to the festival discussed in the text.

section: We Want Bangla as a State Language.
text:
LESSON: We Want Bangla as a State Language.
HISTORICAL NARRATIVE: During the period of Pakistan's rule, the authorities announced that Urdu would be the state language. Most of the people in Pakistan spoke Bangla at that time, but officials still wanted Urdu alone to have state-language status. Bengali speakers insisted that Bangla also be recognized. When the authorities refused, a language-rights movement began. On February 21, 1952, students gathered at the University of Dhaka. The night before, they had written posters saying, "We want Bangla as a state language." The government tried to prevent large gatherings, but students decided to march. The first group of marchers included female students. Others followed with clenched fists and shouted the demand for Bangla. Government forces attacked and shot at protesters. Language activists, including Salam, Barkat, Rafiq and Jabbar, were killed, along with others who remain unnamed. The blood of protesters stained the streets, and the country responded with grief and anger.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Above the prose is a grouped portrait illustration of four male Bengali Language Movement martyrs or activists. Their faces and clothing are drawn against a soft blue background. This page uses portraits to honor people involved in the language movement; it is not a crowd or street-march picture.

section: We Want Bangla as a State Language.
text:
HISTORICAL NARRATIVE CONTINUED: The protests and gatherings continued. Eventually the government accepted Bangla alongside Urdu as an official state language. February 21 is remembered as Shaheed Dibosh, Language Martyrs' Day. It is also observed internationally as International Mother Language Day.
VOCABULARY: rule/govern = administer a country; resentment = displeasure or anger; poster = public notice on a large sheet; slogan = a phrase shouted together during protest; together = assembled; procession or march = people walking together for a cause; gathering = assembling for a purpose; attack = violent assault.
EXERCISE 1: Separate conjunct Bengali consonants from the words for Pakistan, poster and planning; use each pattern in another word.
EXERCISE 2: Create sentences using state language, procession, poster and gathering.

section: Today's Children (Ajikar Shishu). POET: Sufia Kamal. This page prints an excerpt.
text:
LESSON: Today's Children (Ajikar Shishu). POET: Sufia Kamal. This page prints an excerpt.
POEM — ENGLISH RENDERING OF MAIN IDEAS: In the older generation, children played with dolls and listened to fairy tales about jinn, fairies and mysterious underground kingdoms. Today's children learn about machines and travel by modern ships and vehicles, flying toward the sky and crossing the world. Children will move further, explore unknown places, bring knowledge and light into their homes, and drive away ignorance and darkness. They will build bonds of love between people and make the world sweeter and better. The poem contrasts earlier childhood with the present age of science, imagination and collective progress. [Rendered for meaning; parts of the verse and attribution are faint in OCR.]

LESSON: Dhakai Muslin.
STORY FRAME: Mili likes reading books and sometimes reads newspapers. Her father explains that newspapers help us learn new things. One day a newspaper contains an interesting story. The chapter reproduces a piece from the newspaper's "Children's Page."
ARTICLE: Muslin is an old kind of cloth from Bengal. It was world-famous for its very fine thread, lightness, transparency and delicate texture. People said that a muslin sari could pass through a finger ring because it was so fine. The threads were made from a special cotton variety called phuti cotton. Workers used spinning wheels to turn this cotton into thread. Expert weavers wove the fine thread into cloth. Sonargaon near Dhaka was particularly famous for muslin production. The river Shitalakshya's water and the local climate were regarded as suitable for making muslin. Merchants came to purchase muslin. Later, industrially produced factory cloth captured much of the market, and muslin making declined. Researchers and scientists have worked to revive the lost craft, creating new muslin. Muslin is part of Bengal's heritage.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A black rectangular frame surrounds a reproduced newspaper clipping headed "Daily Sakal-Bikal news" and "Children's Page," with a large red headline announcing the return of Dhakai muslin. The article text is arranged in two narrow columns. There is no separate illustration of cloth or a loom on this page.

VOCABULARY: fine = extremely thin or delicate; world-famous = famous throughout the world; thread through = make something pass inside another object.
EXERCISE 1: Break joined Bengali letters into component characters and form related words. Source examples include transparent (swachchha), subtle/fine (sukshma), Shitalakshya, scientist (biggani), and region (anchal).
EXERCISE 2: Understand phuti cotton = a special type of cotton; spinning wheel or charka = a device for spinning thread.
EXERCISE 3: Make sentences using newspaper, famous, factory and competition.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Consonant-joining letter practice, two definitions, and handwriting lines, without a new large illustration.

EXERCISE 4: Answer: (a) What is muslin? (b) How was muslin thread made? (c) Who came to buy muslin? (d) Why did muslin production disappear?

EXERCISE 6: Look at each of the small pictures and write a sentence.

LESSON: Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA).
STORY: It is noon in the desert of Arabia. The sand is so hot that walking is difficult. Hazrat Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) walks across the plain and sees a young man lying on the burning sand, while the young man's owner stands nearby. Abu Bakr asks what the young man has done and why he is being punished. His owner angrily says that the young man is an enslaved person who has accepted Islam. Abu Bakr feels sympathy, buys the young man and sets him free. The young man is Bilal (RA), who becomes the first muezzin in Islam, calling Muslims to prayer in his melodious voice. The story explains that enslaved people faced harsh treatment in Arabia and that Abu Bakr freed many. Abu Bakr was a close companion of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). When opponents threatened Muhammad's life, he migrated from Mecca to Medina, and Abu Bakr accompanied him.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: The upper half shows a wide orange-and-yellow Arabian desert with rolling dunes, sparse palm clusters and a small camel caravan. Several camels carry riders and patterned saddle blankets, walking in a line beneath an orange sun. This is a setting illustration; the event involving the enslaved youth is described in prose rather than drawn in the top picture.

STORY CONTINUED: From childhood Abu Bakr had a compassionate disposition and good character. He sought knowledge. After the death of Prophet Muhammad, he became the first caliph, a leader of the Muslim community. Even as caliph, he remembered people who were poor or in need. He used public funds to care for them. Before his death, he told his daughter Ayesha that a camel and a servant belonging to the state were in his care and should be returned to his successor. He paid attention to the wellbeing of people in servitude and tried to prevent their suffering.
VOCABULARY: plain = wide open land; hot = heated; burning hot = extremely hot; angry = upset; master = owner; enslaved person = person treated as property; muezzin = person who calls people to prayer; call = invitation; companion = associate; hijra/migration = moving from one place to another.
EXERCISE 1: Break the Bengali consonant combinations in words from the lesson and make words with similar combinations.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: The narrative is printed across the upper portion and followed by a glossary and spelling exercises. A small figure shows a person in historical Arabian dress, which supports the lesson's period setting.

EXERCISE 2: Fill blanks: "The sand was ___ in the noon sun"; "Abu Bakr felt ___"; "Bilal's beautiful voice first gave the ___"; "Abu Bakr was a close ___ of Muhammad"; "Opponents once announced they would kill the Prophet"; "Abu Bakr used public funds for the welfare of the ___."
EXERCISE 3: Write sentences with migration, call to prayer, companion, oppression and helpless person.
EXERCISE 4: Learn opposites: hot/cold; punishment/forgiveness; master/servant; welfare/harm; birth/death.
EXERCISE 5: Answer. (a) Who was made to lie on the hot sand? (b) To which city did Prophet Muhammad migrate? (c) Who was the first caliph of Islam? (d) Who was the first muezzin? (e) What instruction did Abu Bakr give his daughter before his death?
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: Five groups of writing exercises with short word banks and ruled spaces; no independent main figure.

EXERCISE 6: Select the correct answer. Who was walking across the scorching sand? [Muhammad, Abu Bakr, Umar, Bilal.] What does "enslaved person" mean? [A person held as property, master, muezzin, caliph.]

LESSON: My Pledge. POET: Madanmohan Tarkalankar.
POEM — ENGLISH RENDERING: Each morning when I wake, I make a promise in my heart. I will act well throughout the day. I will do what my elders instruct with sincerity and diligence. I will not be lazy, cheat or tell lies. I will love all my brothers and sisters and live peacefully with others. I will not quarrel needlessly or yield to greed. I will carry out my tasks with care so that everyone can live happily together. The poem teaches everyday ethical conduct by making a pledge on waking in the morning. [Meaning-based English rendering, not line-for-line rhyme.]
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A sunrise glows through blue clouds on the right. At the bottom, a father in a green kurta holds the shoulder of a small child, another boy sits reading an open book, and a child in a white shirt stands smiling among white flowers. VOCABULARY: instruction/order = command; neglect or laziness = failure to pay attention or act; ever/never = at any time; cheating = deceiving or failing to do an assigned task; elders = older respected people.

LESSON: The Story of Human Kindness (Manob Joyer Golpo) — Nicholas.
STORY: A long time ago, in a village called Patara near the sea in what is now Turkey, a child named Nicholas was born. The passage explains his name as "human victory" or "victory of humanity." His parents were wealthy, but he lost them while still young and grew up an orphan. This helped him understand the sadness of children without parents. He began giving away inherited wealth to people in need. He liked giving presents to children, travelled widely and looked for people who were poor or in distress. His kindness and generous actions made him well known. A tradition developed of giving children gifts on special occasions. Nicholas died on December 6; some countries observe that date as Saint Nicholas Day or Nicholas Day, celebrate with children, give them gifts and share special food.

text:
LESSON: The Palm Tree. POET: Rabindranath Tagore.
POEM — ENGLISH RENDERING: The palm tree stands on one leg, taller than all the other trees, and peeps into the sky. It wishes it could break through the black clouds, but where could it find wings? Its large round leaves seem like a bird's nest or wings. When the wind blows, the leaves shake as though the palm tree is trying to fly somewhere far away. When the wind stops, the leaves settle. Then the tree's longing comes back to the earth. The ground is like its mother, and its roots keep it there. The poem gives a tree a human wish to fly and to return to its mother, the earth.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A long slender palm tree rises above a blue riverbank. Its thin, bare trunk supports a dense crown of green fan-like leaves. A few boats are on the river beside the tree, and low green plants surround its base. The tree towers over everything and its upper leaves almost touch the page's poem heading.

LESSON: Rabindranath Tagore's Childhood.
TEXT: We all know Rabindranath Tagore as a great poet, but he did not enjoy school lessons very much as a child. He felt sleepy when studying at night and sometimes received scoldings from his teacher. His childhood was very lively. He liked wrestling. His wrestling teacher was Kana Palowan, and he practiced every morning. He returned home with dust and mud on his skin. His mother became worried that his skin would become dark from the dirt, so on holidays she scrubbed and washed him thoroughly. The account shows that a famous poet was also once a mischievous, curious child.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A large colored portrait of Rabindranath Tagore as a young adult, with long wavy dark hair, a moustache and a light-colored traditional Bengali shirt. A soft golden background surrounds the head and shoulders. Below the portrait are two paragraphs of biography.

STORY CONTINUED: Young Rabindranath sometimes wished for a fever so that he would not have to study. He would stay in the rain hoping to become sick, but his health was usually strong. In the evening, his mother gathered with the women of the household to tell stories. She would call Rabindranath, who read old books, stories from the Ramayana and interesting scientific accounts to everyone. They were impressed by how much he knew at such a young age. He was particularly interested in a teacher who taught science and was disappointed on days when this teacher did not come. He was surprised to learn that milk contains water and that when milk is heated, some water escapes as vapor so the milk becomes thicker. Later, Tagore became an outstanding poet, songwriter and storyteller. He received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913. A song written by him is Bangladesh's national anthem. He was born on May 7, 1861 (25 Boishakh in the Bengali calendar) and died on August 7, 1941 (22 Srabon).
VOCABULARY: puthi = a traditional written or bound book; astonished = surprised.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A small portrait shows an elderly Rabindranath Tagore with a long gray beard and shawl, seated beside a simple wooden chair with a book or paper. The portrait is placed beneath the final biographical paragraphs.

section: The Ideal Boy. POET: Kusumkumari Das.
text:
LESSON: The Ideal Boy. POET: Kusumkumari Das.
POEM — ENGLISH RENDERING: "What kind of boy does our country need? One who is great not only in words but also through actions. Let his face smile, his chest be brave, his heart full of energy. He must promise to become a good human being. When danger appears, move forward. Do you not have blood, flesh and life in your body? You have hands and feet just like everyone else; why be afraid? Who wants a boy who breaks into tears and holds his head at every little difficulty? Make the promise with a pure heart and a smiling face: I will become a true human being. Every child, whether born in a farmer's home or a king's palace, has work to do and can contribute. With strength in their hands and lives and generous hearts, children can bring welfare to their country." The poem prizes action, courage, kindness and social contribution over empty boasting.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: A child in a green shirt sits at a desk, carefully writing in an open notebook. Several books are stacked on the left and a glass of water stands to the right. LESSON: Rajarbagh in the Liberation War.
STORY: In Dhaka's Rajarbagh area there is a Police Liberation War Museum. Ritu (spelling may be Rita in some editions) learned from her maternal uncle about the events of 1971 at Rajarbagh and wanted to visit. On a holiday, the uncle invites Ritu and her younger brother Robin to the museum. They are delighted. They visit in the afternoon. The museum is tidy and well arranged. At the entrance there is a book counter where visitors can buy books; the uncle buys each child a book. Nearby is a library where readers may sit. After going downstairs to the main museum, they see weapons used by police in different periods, uniforms and other historical objects. The uncle draws their attention to a wireless radio device and a large alarm bell, known as the "pagla ghonta." On the night of March 25, 1971, Pakistani troops attacked Rajarbagh. The police used the wireless set to send warnings to other police units around the country. The alarm bell warned the police at Rajarbagh of the danger.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTION: The museum building is shown from the front as a broad pale-blue and gray structure with a large curved metal roof, glass or open doors, and symmetrical entrance areas. A Bangladesh flag is visible near the entrance. The building photograph-like illustration anchors the narrative to a specific historical museum.

STORY CONTINUED: The police had ordinary weapons but resisted bravely against heavily armed troops. Many police personnel were killed on that night. People from numerous professions joined the Liberation War, ready to risk their lives for independence. Ritu and Robin feel proud when they learn about their courage. Bangladesh's independence was won through such sacrifice.
VOCABULARY: bravery = courage; cannon = a large weapon that fires shells; pride = a sense of honour; weapon = object used in fighting; sacrifice = giving up one's own life for others or for a cause.

LESSON: Write in Your Own Way.
MODEL NARRATIVE: "It was a holiday and I was asleep. Suddenly I heard, 'Meow, meow.' When I woke, there was a little kitten inside the room. I asked, 'What do you want?' The kitten said, 'Meow, meow.' I asked if it was hungry, and it meowed again. I asked, 'What will you eat?' It did not answer. I gave it a bowl of milk. The kitten drank the milk with a lapping sound. I asked, 'Are you full now?' It answered, 'Meow, meow.' I said, 'Meow again!'" This short text is a model for creative storytelling using simple dialogue and sound words.
ILLUSTRATION DESCRIPTIONS: Three stacked rectangular pictures at the right show (1) a nighttime scene with a crescent moon and dark blue sky, (2) a sunny scene with a tree and a bird flying above grass, and (3) a landscape of green plants or fields in the daytime. EXERCISE 1: Write a short passage by filling in words of your choice. Model opening: "It is early morning. A bird is calling. I wonder what the bird is ___ . The bird said, '___.'
